aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute live coding demonstration. Start with a pre-existing VPC and two subnets. First, deploy a simple Nginx EC2 instance. screens.title: Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling
screens.narratorSegment: Today you will learn why Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling are core tools for building resilient web applications. ELB distributes incoming requests across multiple targets so a single failed instance does not take your app offline. Auto Scaling Groups automatically increase or decrease EC2 capacity to meet demand and control cost. Together they maintain availability during traffic spikes and replace unhealthy instances without manual intervention. We'll examine the practical differences between Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers, how listeners, target groups, and health checks work, and how an ASG uses a launch template and scaling policies to adjust capacity. You'll also see developer-focused practices like exposing a meaningful health endpoint and keeping applications stateless so scaling works smoothly. By the end, you should be able to design a simple highly available, auto-scaling web deployment and recognize common misconfigurations, such as overly permissive health checks or too-aggressive scaling rules. To ground this, we'll walk through a deployment pattern that uses an ALB, a target group with a health path, and an ASG with target-tracking scaling. Consider what your application needs to prove healthy before it receives traffic: that is often the difference between a reliable system and one that degrades under load.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Elastic Load Balancing & Auto Scaling

Understand how ELB routes traffic, how ASG adjusts capacity, and why their integration is fundamental to highly available, cost-efficient applications.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you'll use when designing scalable applications. First, you will explain the purpose and benefits of Elastic Load Balancing: how distributing requests across targets protects availability and reduces single points of failure. Second, you will differentiate between Application and Network Load Balancers, so you can choose the right one for HTTP routing or high-performance TCP workloads. Each objective pairs an action with a reason so you know both how and why to use these services. For example, understanding ALB features lets you route A P I requests to serverless backends while sending static asset traffic elsewhere, which simplifies deployments and improves response times. Think of these objectives as developer competencies you can verify by configuring listeners, creating target groups with health checks, and observing traffic behavior under simulated load. We'll show practical configuration examples and a short lab activity so you can demonstrate each competency in a live environment.

screens.title: Developer & Operational Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These additional operational objectives help you design applications that interact well with ELB and ASG. You will learn to expose a health endpoint that reports both server and application readiness so load balancers and Auto Scaling can make good decisions. You will also learn to design services to be stateless or to migrate session state to an external store, because sticky sessions are a brittle fallback. Finally, you will practice defining sensible scaling policies and graceful shutdown so instances complete in-flight requests during termination. Each of these skills reduces downtime risk and prevents common problems like requests routed to instances that appear healthy but cannot reach their database. You will practice by configuring a health path and by reviewing scaling thresholds that avoid thrashing. These operational habits make scaling predictable and safe in production.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Developer Skills

Developer & Operational Skills

Design choices that make autoscaling reliable and predictable in production.

Health Endpoint
Expose /health that checks app dependencies and returns a realistic status. A simple 200 doesn't prove readiness if the DB is down.
Statelessness
Prefer external session stores rather than sticky sessions. Stateless apps scale faster and recover more cleanly.
Graceful Shutdown
Use deregistration delay and trapping of termination signals so in-flight requests finish before instance termination.
Scaling Policies
Use metrics like average CPU, request count per target, or custom CloudWatch metrics and avoid overly aggressive thresholds that cause thrashing.

screens.title: What is Elastic Load Balancing?
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes incoming application traffic across multiple registered targets, such as EC2 instances, containers, or IP addresses, in one or more Availability Zones. The primary purpose is to increase fault tolerance and evenly spread load so no single instance becomes a bottleneck. A concrete example: imagine a web application deployed across three EC2 instances. If traffic surges, ELB will balance new connections among all healthy instances. If one instance fails a health check, ELB will stop sending it traffic while the remaining instances handle requests. A common misconception is thinking ELB eliminates the need to monitor instance health beyond basic checks — ELB performs transport and protocol-level checks, but application-level health must be implemented by the developer. Another misconception is assuming ELB automatically scales compute; ELB distributes traffic but does not add instances — that is the ASG's role. Key developer actions include registering the correct targets, providing an accurate health endpoint that verifies dependencies, and designing for statelessness when possible. In short, ELB is the traffic manager; Auto Scaling manages capacity. When combined they form a resilient, elastic layer that keeps services available under failure and varying load. How will you ensure your health checks reflect real readiness?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is ELB?
Definition

Elastic Load Balancing

Automatically distributes incoming traffic across registered targets and zones to maintain availability and balance load.

  • Supports EC2 instances, containers, IP addresses, and Lambda targets (ALB).
  • Removes unhealthy targets based on health checks so traffic goes only to healthy backends.
  • Works with Auto Scaling to maintain capacity but does not itself scale instances.
Key Takeaway

ELB manages traffic; ensure your health checks reflect true application readiness so ELB routes correctly.

Concrete Example
A website runs on three EC2 instances. ALB listens for HTTP and forwards requests across the three instances. When one instance fails the health check, ALB stops sending traffic to it until the health check returns healthy again.
Misconception
ELB does not auto-scale instances; it only spreads traffic. ASG must add capacity when needed.
Pro tip
Design a /health endpoint that verifies DB connectivity for real readiness checks.

screens.title: ALB, NLB, and GLB — choose the right type
screens.narratorSegment: AWS offers multiple load balancer types and selecting the right one matters for performance and features. The Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and is ideal for HTTP and HTTPS workloads where content-based routing matters. Use ALB when you need to route by URL path, host header, query string, or method, for example sending /api calls to a microservice and /static to a different backend or S3. The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 for high-throughput, low-latency TCP/UDP work and provides static IP addresses — pick NLB for massive connection rates or protocols where header inspection is unnecessary. Gateway Load Balancer acts as a single entry point to deploy virtual appliances like firewalls or intrusion detection systems; it forwards traffic to appliance fleets without requiring each appliance to handle scaling logic. A common mistake is choosing NLB solely for speed when the application requires path-based routing; NLB will not inspect HTTP headers. Conversely, using ALB where session affinity or complex packet handling is needed can cause performance trade-offs. In practice, pick ALB for HTTP microservices and Lambda integrations, NLB for raw TCP performance, and GLB when inserting network appliances. Ask yourself: does my routing decision rely on HTTP content or on raw transport performance?

keyIdea.title: Match the load balancer to the need
keyIdea.text: ALB for Layer 7 routing and microservices, NLB for high-performance transport, GLB for appliance insertion.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › ALB vs NLB vs GLB
Application Load Balancer

Layer 7 routing

Routes by URL, host, headers. Supports containers and Lambda. Use for APIs, microservices, and content-based rules.

Example: route /api/* to API instances and /images/* to an image service.
Network Load Balancer

Layer 4 performance

Ultra-low latency, millions of requests per second, static IPs. Use for TCP, UDP, TLS where header inspection is unnecessary.

Example: a game server using UDP where speed matters more than HTTP routing.
Gateway Load Balancer

Appliance insertion

Deploy and scale virtual appliances like firewalls transparently. Acts as a single entry/exit point for network appliances.

Example: insert a managed intrusion detection service across traffic flows.
Common mistake
Choosing NLB when you actually need content-based routing; NLB won't read HTTP headers.
Takeaway
Match protocol needs and routing features to the right load balancer type to avoid surprises.

screens.title: ALB components: listeners, rules, and target groups
screens.narratorSegment: An Application Load Balancer receives client requests through a listener, applies rules, and forwards traffic to a target group. A listener is a process configured with a protocol and port, for example HTTPS on port 443 or HTTP on port 80. Listener rules evaluate incoming requests and can route based on path patterns, host headers, or other HTTP attributes. When a rule matches, the listener forwards the request to a target group. Target groups define the targets (instances, IPs, or Lambda) and the protocol and port to use. They also include health checks which determine whether a target is eligible to receive traffic. A concrete example: configure an ALB listener for port 80 with two rules — one that routes /api/* to the A P I target group and another that routes /static/* to a static assets group. A common misconception is thinking listeners store routing logic centrally; listeners evaluate rules but the target groups control registration and health status. For developers, ensure target groups use the correct port and protocol and include a health check path that reflects real readiness. When you attach an Auto Scaling Group to an ALB, each launched instance is automatically registered with the specified target group, which completes the request flow from client to app instance.

keyIdea.text: Listeners evaluate rules and forward matched requests to target groups where health checks determine routing eligibility.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Listeners & Target Groups
Core Components

Listener → Rule → Target Group

  • Listener: configured protocol and port, accepts client connections.
  • Rules: path or host-based conditions that decide where to forward traffic.
  • Target Groups: registered targets, port/protocol, and health checks.
Key Takeaway
Correctly map listeners and target groups so requests reach the intended service and unhealthy targets are excluded.
Example Scenario
An ALB listener on port 80 routes /api/* to API target group using HTTP port 8080 on instances while /static/* goes to a target group that points at an S3 endpoint. Health checks use /health and expect a 200 that confirms DB access.
Misconception
Assuming a 200 response is always enough; include dependency checks in readiness endpoints.
Pro tip
Use different target groups per microservice so you can scale and health-check independently.

screens.title: Health Checks: design and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Health checks are the mechanism ELB uses to determine whether targets can safely receive traffic. A well-designed health check endpoint returns a success status only when the application is truly ready — that means verifying upstream dependencies like databases, caches, or external APIs if their absence prevents serving requests. For example, a /health endpoint might check database connectivity and a cache ping before returning success. A common pitfall is a health check that reports OK when a crucial dependency is down; that leaves the load balancer sending traffic to an instance that cannot serve requests. Another mistake is making the health check too heavy by performing slow or costly work, which leads to false negatives and flapping. Configure reasonable intervals, timeouts, and thresholds: for web apps a health check every 30 seconds with short timeouts is common, and healthy/unhealthy threshold counts prevent transient failures from marking instances unhealthy too quickly. Remember that health checks influence both routing and Auto Scaling decisions. If an ASG or ELB sees repeated failures, the ASG may terminate and replace the instance. Finally, implement graceful shutdown and a deregistration delay so an instance leaving service finishes in-flight requests before being removed from rotation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Health Checks

Designing health checks

Health checks decide whether a target receives traffic. They should confirm the application's ability to serve real requests, not just process existence.

Checks to include
  • Database connectivity
  • Cache availability
  • Required third-party APIs
Avoid
Heavy or slow operations, destructive checks, and anything that can cause false negatives on healthy instances.
Configuration
Set intervals, timeouts, and thresholds to balance sensitivity and stability. Use deregistration delay to let in-flight requests finish.
Common Mistake
Returning HTTP 200 without checking downstream services gives a false sense of readiness and leads to errors when traffic reaches the instance.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups: launch templates & lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Scaling Groups ensure you have the desired number of healthy instances running. You define a launch template containing the AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data script. The ASG uses that template to launch instances across Availability Zones according to the group's minimum, maximum, and desired counts. When an instance starts, ASG can automatically register it with an associated target group so the load balancer begins health checking it. If the instance fails health checks or the ASG detects an instance as unhealthy, the ASG may terminate it and launch a replacement to maintain desired capacity. A concrete example: you create a launch template that installs Nginx and serves a static page. You set the ASG desired count to two and the minimum to one. If you attach the ASG to an ALB target group, the new instances will be registered and the ALB will only route traffic when health checks pass. A misconception is thinking ASG scaling is immediate; scaling policies evaluate metrics over configured periods, so brief spikes may not trigger scaling. Also remember to set graceful shutdown and deregistration delay to avoid dropping in-flight requests during termination. The ASG lifecycle makes capacity management predictable when templates and health signals are correct.

keyIdea.title: ASG manages instances
keyIdea.text: Launch templates define instance configuration; ASG ensures desired capacity and registers instances with ELB target groups for health-based routing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Auto Scaling Groups
Process: launch template → ASG config → instance lifecycle
1. Launch Template
AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data to install software.
2. ASG Settings
Min, desired, max capacity and subnet/AZ selection.
3. Registration
ASG registers instances with target groups for the ELB to health-check.
4. Replacement
Unhealthy instances are terminated and replaced automatically.
Key Takeaway
A correct launch template plus health checks and deregistration delay ensures smooth scale and replacement behavior.

screens.title: Infrastructure as Code: Target Group and Listener snippet
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as Code is the recommended way to manage ELB and ASG configurations because it makes changes repeatable and reviewable. Let's walk through a CloudFormation snippet that defines a target group and a listener. The target group sets health check properties like interval, path, protocol, timeout, and thresholds. These values control how quickly unhealthy instances are removed from rotation and how tolerant you are of transient failures. The listener has default actions that forward traffic to the target group. In practice, you will export and reference ARNs and VPC IDs between stacks to keep templates modular. A concrete example is a WebAppTargetGroup configured with a health check path /health, HTTP protocol, 30-second interval, and a matcher that expects HTTP 200. A common misconception is failing to set the target group's correct port or protocol for the application; mismatched ports cause all health checks to fail. When you embed these definitions in your CI/CD pipeline, a code review can catch health-check and listener misconfigurations before they reach production. Read the example and confirm the health check path, port, and protocol reflect the application you deploy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › CloudFormation Snippet
Code
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: ALB Target Group and Listener for a web application

Resources:
  WebAppTargetGroup:
    Type: AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::TargetGroup
    Properties:
      HealthCheckIntervalSeconds: 30
      HealthCheckPath: /health
      HealthCheckProtocol: HTTP
      HealthCheckTimeoutSeconds: 5
      HealthyThresholdCount: 2
      Matcher:
        HttpCode: '200'
      Name: WebAppTargetGroup
      Port: 80
      Protocol: HTTP
      TargetType: instance
      UnhealthyThresholdCount: 2
      VpcId: !ImportValue MyVPCId

  ALBListener:
    Type: AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::Listener
    Properties:
      DefaultActions:
        - Type: forward
          TargetGroupArn: !Ref WebAppTargetGroup
      LoadBalancerArn: !ImportValue MyALBArn
      Port: 80
      Protocol: HTTP
What to check
Ensure HealthCheckPath and Matcher match your app response and port matches the app listening port.
Why IaC
Templates are auditable and deployable via CI/CD so configuration drifts are minimized.
Pitfall
Exporting wrong VPC or ALB ARN between stacks causes unresolved references and failed deployments.

screens.title: Integrating ELB with Auto Scaling Groups
screens.narratorSegment: When you attach an Auto Scaling Group to an ELB target group, the ASG automatically registers launched instances and deregisters instances that are terminated. This integration ensures new capacity becomes available to serve traffic as soon as it passes health checks. Scaling policies determine when the ASG launches or terminates instances — common policies are target-tracking based on average C P U utilization, or step scaling that reacts to bursts. Lifecycle hooks let you run custom actions during launch or termination, for example running a script to warm caches or draining connections before termination. A concrete scenario: set a target-tracking policy to keep average C P U at 50 percent. If C P U rises and remains above the target for the configured evaluation period, the ASG will scale out, launching new instances via the launch template, each automatically registering with the target group. Misconfiguration can cause issues: if the health check path is wrong, new instances might register but remain unhealthy and never serve traffic. Another problem is thrashing — overly aggressive scale-in and scale-out actions. Use cooldowns, evaluation periods, and step scaling to make scaling decisions stable. Think about what pre-warm actions you need so a newly launched instance can pass health checks quickly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › ASG & ELB Integration

Automatic registration flow

Launch template creates instance → ASG launches instance → ASG registers instance with target group → ALB health checks begin → instance receives traffic when healthy.
Lifecycle Hooks
Run custom tasks during launch/termination for warming or graceful drain.
Cooldowns
Prevent rapid scale actions by using cooldown periods and evaluation windows.
Example: scaling policy

screens.title: Developer considerations: stateless design and sticky sessions
screens.narratorSegment: Design choices at the application layer influence how effectively ELB and ASG work. Stateless services are simplest to scale because any instance can handle any request. If your app stores session state in memory, scaling or replacing instances will lose user sessions and force workarounds like sticky sessions. Sticky sessions provide session affinity but introduce risks: they can concentrate traffic on fewer instances, reduce effective elasticity, and complicate replacement. A preferable approach is to externalize state to a shared store such as a cache or database so instances remain interchangeable. Developers should also expose a health endpoint that checks critical dependencies and ensure the endpoint is lightweight and fast. Another consideration is readiness versus liveness checks: readiness indicates the app can serve requests, while liveness shows the process is running. Using both appropriately prevents routing traffic to instances that are up but not ready. For graceful termination, trap the termination signal in your app and allow in-flight requests to complete before shutting down. These patterns make autoscaling behavior smooth and predictable and prevent user-visible errors during scale events. How will you adapt your app so instances can be safely replaced at any time?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Developer Considerations

Stateless vs sticky sessions

Stateless services allow any instance to serve any request. Sticky sessions bind a client to an instance, which can limit scaling and create single points of load.
Stateless pattern
Move session data to external stores like caches so instances are interchangeable.
Sticky session tradeoffs
Use only when necessary; understand it reduces elasticity and complicates maintenance.
Graceful shutdown
Trap termination signals, deregister from ELB, wait for deregistration delay to finish in-flight requests, then exit.

screens.title: Deploy a scalable web app: lab walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This activity outlines the steps to deploy a simple Nginx web app behind an ALB and an Auto Scaling Group so you can practice the integration. Start with a VPC and at least two public subnets in different Availability Zones. Create a launch template that installs Nginx via user data and writes an index page. Then create an ALB with a security group that allows HTTP, create a target group with HealthCheckPath set to / and attach it to the ALB listener on port 80. Next, create an Auto Scaling Group that uses the launch template, selects both subnets, and attaches to the ALB and target group. Set desired capacity to two, min to one, and max to four. Configure a target-tracking scaling policy for average C P U utilization at 50 percent. After creation, verify instances register with the target group and become healthy. Access the ALB DNS to see the Nginx page. To test scaling, generate load and observe the ASG scale out; then stop the load and watch scale-in. A common mistake is forgetting to open the ALB's security group to HTTP or setting the ASG to private subnets without NAT access if user data needs external downloads. This lab teaches the end-to-end flow and reinforces why health checks and graceful deregistration matter.

keyIdea.text: Create a launch template, ALB, target group, and ASG with a scaling policy; verify instances register and serve traffic.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Lab Walkthrough

Step-by-step

  1. Create VPC with two public subnets in separate AZs.
  2. Create Launch Template named WebAppLaunchTemplate and add user data to install Nginx.
  3. Create ALB in the VPC, select both public subnets, and allow HTTP in its security group.
  4. Create Target Group (WebAppTargetGroup) with HealthCheckPath '/'.
  5. Create ASG (MyWebAppASG) using the launch template, attach to ALB and target group, set desired 2, min 1, max 4.
  6. Configure target-tracking scaling policy with target CPU 50% and verify behavior under load.
Checklist
Open ALB security group to HTTP, ensure user data can download packages, use proper health path and deregistration delay, and monitor ASG activity during tests.
Success check
ALB DNS returns the Nginx page and target group shows instances healthy.

screens.title: Avoiding scale thrashing and registration errors
screens.narratorSegment: Two frequent operational problems are thrashing and registration errors. Thrashing happens when scaling policies trigger rapid scale out and scale in cycles, often caused by overly-sensitive alarms or too-short evaluation windows. For example, an alarm that requires C P U above 70 percent for only one evaluation period might fire repeatedly on brief spikes. To avoid thrashing, increase the evaluation period, use target-tracking or step-scaling policies, and set cooldown windows. Registration errors occur when new instances register with a target group but fail health checks because the application hasn't finished initialization or required external resources are unreachable. Prevent this by using user data to run initialization tasks, implement readiness checks that only return success when warm, and use deregistration delay and lifecycle hooks to drain traffic before termination. Another misconfiguration is forgetting to set the correct target port or protocol, which causes all health checks to fail. Monitor CloudWatch metrics for TargetResponseTime, HealthyHostCount, and ASG ActivityHistory to spot unusual patterns early. Finally, test termination handling so in-flight requests are not dropped when instances are de-registered or terminated. Avoiding scale thrashing and registration errors means use appropriate evaluation periods, cooldowns, lifecycle hooks, and readiness checks to prevent thrashing and registration failures.. In practical terms, tuning policies, thresholds, and deregistration delays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Pitfalls

Common operational pitfalls

Thrashing
Avoid too-short alarm periods and set cooldowns. Consider step-scaling for sudden spikes.
Registration Failures
Ensure user data completes and readiness checks return success only when the app can serve requests.
Misconfigured Ports
Target group port must match the application listening port; a mismatch leads to failed health checks.
Monitoring
Watch HealthyHostCount and ASG activity to detect noisy scaling or registration problems promptly.
Action
When you see rapid scale events, investigate alarm thresholds and consider smoothing metrics or adding step policies.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts: Elastic Load Balancing distributes incoming application traffic across multiple targets and relies on health checks to route only to healthy backends. Application Load Balancers operate at Layer 7 and support content-based routing, Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 for high-throughput scenarios, and Gateway Load Balancers let you insert virtual appliances. Listeners and target groups form the core ALB configuration: listeners accept connections, rules forward based on request attributes, and target groups define targets and health checks. Auto Scaling Groups use launch templates to create instances and maintain desired capacity, and they integrate with ELB by registering instances automatically. Finally, developer considerations such as stateless design, meaningful readiness checks, graceful shutdown, and sensible scaling policies make these services effective and predictable. Keep these concepts in mind when designing, deploying, and operating scalable applications.

fullNarratorScript:
Today you will learn why Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling are core tools for building resilient web applications. ELB distributes incoming requests across multiple targets so a single failed instance does not take your app offline. Auto Scaling Groups automatically increase or decrease EC2 capacity to meet demand and control cost. Together they maintain availability during traffic spikes and replace unhealthy instances without manual intervention. We'll examine the practical differences between Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers, how listeners, target groups, and health checks work, and how an ASG uses a launch template and scaling policies to adjust capacity. You'll also see developer-focused practices like exposing a meaningful health endpoint and keeping applications stateless so scaling works smoothly. By the end, you should be able to design a simple highly available, auto-scaling web deployment and recognize common misconfigurations, such as overly permissive health checks or too-aggressive scaling rules. To ground this, we'll walk through a deployment pattern that uses an ALB, a target group with a health path, and an ASG with target-tracking scaling. Consider what your application needs to prove healthy before it receives traffic: that is often the difference between a reliable system and one that degrades under load.

These objectives map to practical skills you'll use when designing scalable applications. First, you will explain the purpose and benefits of Elastic Load Balancing: how distributing requests across targets protects availability and reduces single points of failure. Second, you will differentiate between Application and Network Load Balancers, so you can choose the right one for HTTP routing or high-performance TCP workloads. Each objective pairs an action with a reason so you know both how and why to use these services. For example, understanding ALB features lets you route A P I requests to serverless backends while sending static asset traffic elsewhere, which simplifies deployments and improves response times. Think of these objectives as developer competencies you can verify by configuring listeners, creating target groups with health checks, and observing traffic behavior under simulated load. We'll show practical configuration examples and a short lab activity so you can demonstrate each competency in a live environment.

These additional operational objectives help you design applications that interact well with ELB and ASG. You will learn to expose a health endpoint that reports both server and application readiness so load balancers and Auto Scaling can make good decisions. You will also learn to design services to be stateless or to migrate session state to an external store, because sticky sessions are a brittle fallback. Finally, you will practice defining sensible scaling policies and graceful shutdown so instances complete in-flight requests during termination. Each of these skills reduces downtime risk and prevents common problems like requests routed to instances that appear healthy but cannot reach their database. You will practice by configuring a health path and by reviewing scaling thresholds that avoid thrashing. These operational habits make scaling predictable and safe in production.

Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes incoming application traffic across multiple registered targets, such as EC2 instances, containers, or IP addresses, in one or more Availability Zones. The primary purpose is to increase fault tolerance and evenly spread load so no single instance becomes a bottleneck. A concrete example: imagine a web application deployed across three EC2 instances. If traffic surges, ELB will balance new connections among all healthy instances. If one instance fails a health check, ELB will stop sending it traffic while the remaining instances handle requests. A common misconception is thinking ELB eliminates the need to monitor instance health beyond basic checks — ELB performs transport and protocol-level checks, but application-level health must be implemented by the developer. Another misconception is assuming ELB automatically scales compute; ELB distributes traffic but does not add instances — that is the ASG's role. Key developer actions include registering the correct targets, providing an accurate health endpoint that verifies dependencies, and designing for statelessness when possible. In short, ELB is the traffic manager; Auto Scaling manages capacity. When combined they form a resilient, elastic layer that keeps services available under failure and varying load. How will you ensure your health checks reflect real readiness?

AWS offers multiple load balancer types and selecting the right one matters for performance and features. The Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and is ideal for HTTP and HTTPS workloads where content-based routing matters. Use ALB when you need to route by URL path, host header, query string, or method, for example sending /api calls to a microservice and /static to a different backend or S3. The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 for high-throughput, low-latency TCP/UDP work and provides static IP addresses — pick NLB for massive connection rates or protocols where header inspection is unnecessary. Gateway Load Balancer acts as a single entry point to deploy virtual appliances like firewalls or intrusion detection systems; it forwards traffic to appliance fleets without requiring each appliance to handle scaling logic. A common mistake is choosing NLB solely for speed when the application requires path-based routing; NLB will not inspect HTTP headers. Conversely, using ALB where session affinity or complex packet handling is needed can cause performance trade-offs. In practice, pick ALB for HTTP microservices and Lambda integrations, NLB for raw TCP performance, and GLB when inserting network appliances. Ask yourself: does my routing decision rely on HTTP content or on raw transport performance?

An Application Load Balancer receives client requests through a listener, applies rules, and forwards traffic to a target group. A listener is a process configured with a protocol and port, for example HTTPS on port 443 or HTTP on port 80. Listener rules evaluate incoming requests and can route based on path patterns, host headers, or other HTTP attributes. When a rule matches, the listener forwards the request to a target group. Target groups define the targets (instances, IPs, or Lambda) and the protocol and port to use. They also include health checks which determine whether a target is eligible to receive traffic. A concrete example: configure an ALB listener for port 80 with two rules — one that routes /api/* to the A P I target group and another that routes /static/* to a static assets group. A common misconception is thinking listeners store routing logic centrally; listeners evaluate rules but the target groups control registration and health status. For developers, ensure target groups use the correct port and protocol and include a health check path that reflects real readiness. When you attach an Auto Scaling Group to an ALB, each launched instance is automatically registered with the specified target group, which completes the request flow from client to app instance.

Health checks are the mechanism ELB uses to determine whether targets can safely receive traffic. A well-designed health check endpoint returns a success status only when the application is truly ready — that means verifying upstream dependencies like databases, caches, or external APIs if their absence prevents serving requests. For example, a /health endpoint might check database connectivity and a cache ping before returning success. A common pitfall is a health check that reports OK when a crucial dependency is down; that leaves the load balancer sending traffic to an instance that cannot serve requests. Another mistake is making the health check too heavy by performing slow or costly work, which leads to false negatives and flapping. Configure reasonable intervals, timeouts, and thresholds: for web apps a health check every 30 seconds with short timeouts is common, and healthy/unhealthy threshold counts prevent transient failures from marking instances unhealthy too quickly. Remember that health checks influence both routing and Auto Scaling decisions. If an ASG or ELB sees repeated failures, the ASG may terminate and replace the instance. Finally, implement graceful shutdown and a deregistration delay so an instance leaving service finishes in-flight requests before being removed from rotation.

Auto Scaling Groups ensure you have the desired number of healthy instances running. You define a launch template containing the AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data script. The ASG uses that template to launch instances across Availability Zones according to the group's minimum, maximum, and desired counts. When an instance starts, ASG can automatically register it with an associated target group so the load balancer begins health checking it. If the instance fails health checks or the ASG detects an instance as unhealthy, the ASG may terminate it and launch a replacement to maintain desired capacity. A concrete example: you create a launch template that installs Nginx and serves a static page. You set the ASG desired count to two and the minimum to one. If you attach the ASG to an ALB target group, the new instances will be registered and the ALB will only route traffic when health checks pass. A misconception is thinking ASG scaling is immediate; scaling policies evaluate metrics over configured periods, so brief spikes may not trigger scaling. Also remember to set graceful shutdown and deregistration delay to avoid dropping in-flight requests during termination. The ASG lifecycle makes capacity management predictable when templates and health signals are correct.

Infrastructure as Code is the recommended way to manage ELB and ASG configurations because it makes changes repeatable and reviewable. Let's walk through a CloudFormation snippet that defines a target group and a listener. The target group sets health check properties like interval, path, protocol, timeout, and thresholds. These values control how quickly unhealthy instances are removed from rotation and how tolerant you are of transient failures. The listener has default actions that forward traffic to the target group. In practice, you will export and reference ARNs and VPC IDs between stacks to keep templates modular. A concrete example is a WebAppTargetGroup configured with a health check path /health, HTTP protocol, 30-second interval, and a matcher that expects HTTP 200. A common misconception is failing to set the target group's correct port or protocol for the application; mismatched ports cause all health checks to fail. When you embed these definitions in your CI/CD pipeline, a code review can catch health-check and listener misconfigurations before they reach production. Read the example and confirm the health check path, port, and protocol reflect the application you deploy.

When you attach an Auto Scaling Group to an ELB target group, the ASG automatically registers launched instances and deregisters instances that are terminated. This integration ensures new capacity becomes available to serve traffic as soon as it passes health checks. Scaling policies determine when the ASG launches or terminates instances — common policies are target-tracking based on average C P U utilization, or step scaling that reacts to bursts. Lifecycle hooks let you run custom actions during launch or termination, for example running a script to warm caches or draining connections before termination. A concrete scenario: set a target-tracking policy to keep average C P U at 50 percent. If C P U rises and remains above the target for the configured evaluation period, the ASG will scale out, launching new instances via the launch template, each automatically registering with the target group. Misconfiguration can cause issues: if the health check path is wrong, new instances might register but remain unhealthy and never serve traffic. Another problem is thrashing — overly aggressive scale-in and scale-out actions. Use cooldowns, evaluation periods, and step scaling to make scaling decisions stable. Think about what pre-warm actions you need so a newly launched instance can pass health checks quickly.

Using both appropriately prevents routing traffic to instances that are up but not ready.
